<description>
{
 "summary": "Fixes request body deserialization for the `/rest/getutxos` POST endpoint. Rather than writing the request string into a `DataStream` with `operator<<`, which prepended a `CompactSize` length prefix, the endpoint parses body bytes in place using `SpanReader`. The change also caps vector deserialization at `MAX_GETUTXOS_OUTPOINTS`, rejects trailing unparsed bytes with an HTTP 400 error, and fails malformed hex inputs using `TryParseHex`.",
 "problem": "Binary and hex POST requests to `/rest/getutxos` incorrectly report that valid outpoints do not exist. Serializing the body string with `operator<<` inserts a length prefix, causing the parser to interpret the length byte as the `checkmempool` flag and misalign all subsequent outpoints. In addition, an unbounded vector read could allocate memory for large declared counts before reaching the 15-outpoint validation check, and trailing or malformed data was silently accepted.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'Binary GET and POST requests to /rest/getutxos for the same outpoints should agree. GET finds the unspent output, but POST incorrectly reports no hit.'",
  "Commit 57dc676b59: 'Writing the POST body to DataStream with operator<< serializes it as a string and prepends a CompactSize length, which the parser incorrectly reads as request fields.'"

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
